---
title: "Parameterized Quarto Reports"
date: 2026-10-31
description: "Using one Quarto template to create customized R reports while keeping interactive development practical."
categories: [Quarto, R, reproducibility]
---

## Question

How can one `.qmd` file produce several customized reports without making the
document awkward to develop interactively?

The key is to separate three things:

1. **The template** defines and uses parameters.
2. **The render command** can override their default values.
3. **An interactive helper** loads the defaults when code cells are run outside
   a render.

Quarto and Knitr use the name `params` (plural). During a render, Knitr creates
this list before executing the document. Running an individual R cell does not
perform that render setup, so `params` may not exist in the interactive R
session.

## A minimal template

Define sensible defaults in the document's YAML:

````markdown
---
title: "Regional Sales Report"
params:
  region: "Midwest"
  start_date: "2026-01-01"
  include_detail: false
---

```r
#| echo: false

region <- params$region
start_date <- as.Date(params$start_date)
include_detail <- params$include_detail
```
````

Defaults are useful even when production renders always override them: the
document remains runnable, and the defaults document the expected parameter
names and types.

### Render with the defaults

```bash
quarto render report.qmd
```

The editor's Preview or Render button also uses these defaults unless the
editor has been configured to call Quarto with overrides.

### Override values at the command line

```bash
quarto render report.qmd \
  -P region:West \
  -P start_date:2026-07-01 \
  -P include_detail:true
```

`-P` is short for `--execute-param`. Repeating it is convenient for a few
values.

### Keep a named set of values in YAML

For repeatable report variants, put only the overrides in a separate file:

```yaml
# west.yml
region: "West"
start_date: "2026-07-01"
include_detail: true
```

Then render with:

```bash
quarto render report.qmd --execute-params west.yml
```

This is easier to review and reuse than a long command. Do not store passwords,
tokens, or other secrets in a parameter file committed to Git.

## Interactive development

A small utility can read the template's default parameters when `params` does
not already exist. The guard matters: during a real render, it preserves the
values supplied by Quarto instead of replacing them with defaults.

```r
read_quarto_params <- function(input) {
  yaml_params <- rmarkdown::yaml_front_matter(input)$params

  if (is.null(yaml_params)) {
    stop("No `params` section found in ", input, call. = FALSE)
  }

  lapply(yaml_params, function(parameter) {
    if (is.list(parameter) && "value" %in% names(parameter)) {
      parameter$value
    } else {
      parameter
    }
  })
}
```

Near the beginning of `report.qmd`, use the helper only as an interactive
fallback:

```r
if (!exists("params", inherits = FALSE)) {
  source("R/read-quarto-params.R")
  params <- read_quarto_params("report.qmd")
}
```

This helper loads **YAML defaults**, not command-line overrides. That is a
feature: interactive work gets a predictable example configuration, while a
render remains the authoritative test of a customized report. To explore a
different case interactively, change selected values explicitly:

```r
params$region <- "West"
```

## Validate early

Parameters are inputs to the analysis. Check them once in a setup cell so a
bad render fails with a useful message rather than producing a plausible but
wrong report.

```r
required_params <- c("region", "start_date", "include_detail")
missing_params <- setdiff(required_params, names(params))

if (length(missing_params) > 0) {
  stop("Missing parameters: ", paste(missing_params, collapse = ", "))
}

allowed_regions <- c("Midwest", "Northeast", "South", "West")
if (!params$region %in% allowed_regions) {
  stop("Unknown region: ", params$region)
}

start_date <- as.Date(params$start_date)
if (is.na(start_date)) {
  stop("`start_date` must use YYYY-MM-DD format")
}

if (!is.logical(params$include_detail) || length(params$include_detail) != 1) {
  stop("`include_detail` must be one TRUE or FALSE value")
}
```

Keeping dates in YAML as quoted ISO strings and converting them in R makes the
type contract visible and avoids relying on a YAML parser's implicit date
conversion.

## Produce several reports from R

The `quarto` R package can pass a named list through `execute_params`. Give each
render a distinct output filename so one variant does not overwrite another.

```r
regions <- c("Midwest", "West")

for (region in regions) {
  quarto::quarto_render(
    input = "report.qmd",
    output_file = paste0("sales-", tolower(region), ".html"),
    execute_params = list(
      region = region,
      start_date = "2026-07-01",
      include_detail = FALSE
    )
  )
}
```

Parameterized rendering is usually enough for a modest reporting workflow. If
the number of reports, dependencies, or scheduling rules grows substantially,
a pipeline tool such as `targets` may become a better orchestration layer.

## What I learned

- A parameterized document is a function-like template: YAML supplies defaults,
  and each render supplies inputs.
- `params` exists during Knitr rendering, not automatically during interactive
  cell execution.
- A guarded helper makes interactive work convenient without changing render
  behavior.
- Parameter values should control analysis choices, not contain secrets or
  replace input validation.
- A customized report is only verified when it is rendered with the intended
  overrides; successfully running cells with defaults is not the same test.
- Parameters control computation. Quarto metadata such as `format`, `toc`, and
  `output-file` controls document rendering, even though both are written in
  YAML.
